newsitem.title: USA: Two top executives ousted at EMI - industry sources.
newsitem.headline: Two top executives ousted at EMI - industry sources.

text.p: The chairman of EMI Group Plc's North American division and another top executive at the label were dismissed as part of a shake-up at the company, industry sources said Saturday.

"Koppelman's out," said one source familiar with the company. Officials at EMI were unavailable for comment on the status of Charles Koppelman, chairman of the North American division, and Terri Santisi, executive vice president.
Another industry source with ties to the label, which is home to the Beatles catalog, said he believed Koppelman's ouster had been in the works for several weeks.

"It's not surprising because EMI's management looked to Koppelman as the principal architect of its day to day music and whenever there are disparities in overall performance, the blame falls on that person," said Thomas White, a representative for the estates of performers, including Fred Astaire and Orson Welles.
EMI's market share fell in 1996 but the label has improved its performance lately with hits at its Virgin label and Capital Records label.

Koppelman took over EMI's North American division in 1992 shortly after selling the corporation his own SBK Record label. Within months, he forced the exit of several well-respected executives and staff at Capitol Records.
"Koppelman has many detractors among people who knew him from previous dealings in the business," White said.
Koppelman hired Gary Gersh, a talent scout to run the Capitol label. Santisi, one of the highest ranking women in the music industry, also joined at Koppelman's urging, industry sources said.
Recently, she played a key role in helping Koppelman restructure the catalog and distribution operations.
One industry source speculated that more executive departures would follow.

In addition, there has been widespread speculation that EMI Music parent Thorn EMI plans to sell the record company. Walt Disney Co. and Seagram Co Ltd's Universal are frequently named as likely suitors.
Spokesman at both companies have declined comment on these rumors and industry sources say the companies view the current $9 billion price tag for EMI as too high.
